messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 58
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Dentist
- Trauma Type: Police violence
- Pcl5: 77

# The Weight of What He Saw

Marcus is a 58-year-old dentist who has built his practice over three decades in a mid-sized Midwestern city. He is known among his patients as steady-handed and calm, the kind of man who can talk a frightened person through a root canal with quiet authority. His partner of eleven years, Diane, describes him the same way — unflappable, deliberate, someone who thinks before he speaks. That is who Marcus was before the afternoon of a Saturday in late spring, two years ago, when he watched a police officer kill his nephew on the street outside a convenience store.

Marcus had driven his nephew, Darnell, twenty-three years old and recently enrolled in a community college automotive program, to pick up a few things before a family cookout. Marcus waited in the car. He heard shouting first, then watched through the windshield as two officers confronted Darnell on the sidewalk. The encounter escalated in seconds. Marcus was still reaching for his door handle when the shots were fired. He ran to Darnell and held him on the pavement until the ambulance arrived. Darnell did not survive. Marcus's hands, the same hands he uses every day to repair and restore, were covered in his nephew's blood.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus told himself he was managing. He attended the funeral, gave a eulogy, supported his sister through her grief. He returned to his practice after ten days because he said the work would help him focus. But his patients began to notice something different. He startled at unexpected sounds — the suction equipment, a dropped instrument tray. He found himself staring at his gloved hands between procedures, unable to account for the lost minutes. His dental assistant, a woman who has worked with him for fifteen years, quietly started handling more of the patient communication because Marcus had become terse in ways he didn't seem to recognize.

At home, sleep became a negotiation he almost always lost. He lies down beside Diane and waits. When sleep finally comes, it delivers him back to the sidewalk — the sound, the pavement, the specific quality of afternoon light. He wakes drenched and disoriented, sometimes sitting up with his hands pressed flat against the mattress as though checking that the surface beneath him is solid. Diane reaches for him and he lets her, but he has told her almost nothing about what plays out in those dreams. He says he doesn't want to put it in her head too.

During the day, Marcus avoids driving past the neighborhood where it happened. He has rerouted his commute by twelve minutes. He no longer watches local news. When a patient mentions anything about police — a traffic stop, a crime story — he feels his chest tighten and has to concentrate on keeping his hands from trembling. He is acutely aware of how much control his work demands of him, and the awareness itself has become exhausting.

What troubles Marcus most, though he has only recently found words for it, is a creeping sense that the world has revealed something about itself that cannot be unseen. He was 58 years old and believed, in some working way, that if you were careful and respectable and present, the people you loved would be safe. That belief is gone. He moves through his days with a vigilance that never fully releases — scanning parking lots, tracking the position of strangers, calculating exits. He is present in his operatory, precise with his instruments, professional in every observable way. But some part of him is still on that sidewalk, still reaching for the door handle, still arriving three seconds too late.

He has started seeing a therapist at Diane's urging. In their first session, when asked what brought him in, he was quiet for a long moment before he said, simply: *"I can't get my hands clean."*
